title: Object members and operator overloading
body: Every type derives from `object`, which supplies `ToString`, `Equals`, `GetHashCode` and `GetType`. Override `ToString` to produce readable output for logs and debugging; interpolation and `Console.WriteLine` call it automatically.

A type can define operators as `public static` methods: `public static Vector operator +(Vector a, Vector b)`. Overload operators only when the meaning is obvious (numbers, vectors, money). Some operators come in required pairs: `==` with `!=`, `<` with `>`, `<=` with `>=`.

Conversion operators define casts. An `implicit` conversion should never lose information or throw; an `explicit` one is for conversions that can. A `Celsius` to `double` conversion can be explicit to make the unit change visible at call sites.

C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment operators. Before C# 14, `a += b` always meant `a = a + b`, creating a new object. Now a class can declare an instance `public void operator +=(Vector other)` that mutates in place, which avoids allocations for large mutable types. Types without it keep the old behaviour.

Operators must not surprise readers: `+` should not have side effects, and an in-place `+=` must leave the object consistent with what `+` would produce. Check that equality operators agree with `Equals` and that conversions say clearly whether they can lose data.
challenge: Create a readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount, string Currency) with a + operator that throws InvalidOperationException when currencies differ. Print 5 USD + 7 USD and the message for USD + EUR.
solutionStdout:
12 USD
Cannot add USD to EUR
question: In C# 14, what can `public void operator +=(int value)` on a class achieve that `operator +` cannot?
correct: Update the existing object in place instead of creating a new one
wrong: Make + and += have unrelated meanings legally required
Allow += on types that have no + operator only at runtime
reasoning: User-defined compound assignment lets mutable types avoid allocating a new result for every +=.
